newsitem.title: GERMANY: Intel sees ventures priming PC demand.
newsitem.headline: Intel sees ventures priming PC demand.

text.p: Computer chip maker Intel Corp. is reaching well beyond microprocessor manufacturing to pump up future demand for personal computers.

While so many other companies are trying to boost profit by focusing on core businesses, the chip giant is branching into a satellite venture that could eventually feed movies, television and Internet multimedia services directly to desktop computers.

The stake in European Satellite Multimedia Services S.A., announced on Wednesday at the CeBIT computer fair, is the latest step in a strategy of priming PC demand by backing advanced in areas like computer system design, networking technology and Internet telephones.
"Faster modems, communications networks, 3-D visualisation -- anything that brings data bits to the PC, we love it," Pat Gelsinger, Intel's desktop products chief, told Reuters.
With PCs about to become the top-selling electronics device ahead of TV sets, Intel aims to keep demand for its microchips soaring by improving the things computers do now, and fleshing out new uses.

EMS, which is majority-owned by Luxembourg's Societe Europeenne des Satellites, would give media companies a way of broadcasting digital multimedia content to home and business PCs at data rates much faster than telephone lines can support, Intel and SES said at a CeBIT news conference.
High-speed transmissions should open up new applications for home entertainment devices -- with Intel chips inside.

"We want to use Europe's satellite network to support high-speed data transmission to personal computers," said Intel Europe chief Hans Geyer. "Tens of millions of people will be able to communicate by computer. The problem is that getting infromation is limited by data transmission speed."

The EMS service, due to begin operating later this year, would be able to transmit 10 megabytes of data -- enough for a short video clip -- in 2.2 seconds. Today's fastest ISDN telephone lines would require 22 minutes.

Backed by an initial investment of $15 million, EMS planned to first develop services aimed at businesses that already use satellites networks. Later home users could add a $200 connector to link their PCs to a standard 50-centimeter satellite dish.

"You can imagine the contents of a VCR tape being sent to a PC over our network," said Romain Bausch of SES, whose six-satellite network already distributes data for many European TV and cable companies. "There is a tremendous opportunity."

While waiting for EMS to take off, Intel hopes to keep corporate PC purchases rolling by pushing a design for NetPCs -- computers that can be automatically monitored, reset and updated with new software over a network.
These features, offered in a PC design Intel unveiled at CeBIT, should help companies shave thousands of dollars in PC maintenance costs, Gelsinger said.

Scores of PC makers -- including firms like Compaq Computer Corp. that were once renowned for their own prowess at system design -- were readying full lines of NetPCs for release next month, Gelsinger said.

Designing computers to help PC makers offer new technology quickly at attractive prices is a familiar Intel strategy. When it introduced its Pentium chip, Intel produced a design so that PC makers could offer Pentium PCs for about $2,500 -- less than half the price of PCs with brand new chips ten years ago.

While Intel's chip operation forges ahead -- it's due to release a top-performaing Pentium II chip in the next few months -- the company has other groups ranging into areas like modem chips, video conferencing software and kits that let users place phone calls over the Internet.
"In the next two years, PCs will begin outselling TVs," he said. "We don't want the growth to stop there."
